publications.title: Project-Based and Self-Directed Learning
publications.subtitle: Third International Conference on Higher Education Advances, Editorial Universitat Politecnica de Valencia
publications.description: This article discusses the benefits of project-based and self-directed learning to develop competency in utilizing a second language and working collaboratively. The background premise of these modes of learning is provided, demonstrating that they work well for differentiated levels and language skills and improve student competence. Some of the areas examined are intercultural and scientific, ones that require the use of specific language in context. In addition, the concept of creating projects that increase student investment and motivation to make learning more relevant is juxtaposed with a student’s competency in an area after having participated in traditional approaches to learning. The overall benefit of the use of project-based and self-directed learning is that it allows the student to develop a higher skill set and greater engagement with the subject matter, producing better languageand content outcomes.

Every child deserves interventions grounded in evidence, not just good intentions. That's why, after 17 years away from the classroom, I returned to pursue my Masters in the Department of Counselling and Human Development Studies at the University of Ibadan, specializing in Adolescent Psychology and Youth Counselling. My goal is simple: to become an even more effective advocate for street-connected children and vulnerable young people. For over a decade, I've worked with children whose lives have been shaped by poverty, neglect, abuse, and life on the streets. That work demands more than passion, it requires evidence-based practice, deeper psychological understanding, and stronger leadership skill. So, I intentionally sat in the front row, soaking in every lecture from courses such as Creativity and Innovation, Psychology of Adjustment, Organizational Behaviour, Developmental Psychology, Conflict Resolution, Theories of Career Development , and many others. Then came the examinations! Unlike many professional programmes where attendance earns you a certificate, a Masters degree requires you to prove you've truly learned through rigorous achievement tests. And the University of Ibadan is certainly not taking that lightly. So, I have to study to show myself approved unto God and man😁 Is it a walk in the park? Hell No! Seventeen years ago, my biggest responsibility was passing my exams. Today, I study while leading h_streetkidsinitiative , ensuring salaries are paid, checking on the children at Agape Home (our shelter for children in street situations), making sure the kitchen keeps running, and responding to the demands of leadership. Yet, by God's grace, whenever it's time to study, every other thing simply fizzles out. One course after another, I'm signing out of 12 courses that have stretched my mind and sharpened my practice. One semester will soon be done and dusted... two more to go! I'm looking forward to sharing some of the lessons from this journey because when those of us serving vulnerable children continue to learn, the children we serve ultimately benefit. #StreetConnectedChildren #ChildProtection #AdolescentPsychology #YouthCounselling #NonprofitLeadership #UniversityOfIbadan #MastersJourney #EvidenceBasedPractice #SocialImpact

How are group norms in Japan shifting today? I had the opportunity to explore this question at the Consulate General of Japan with my Showa Boston Leadership students and Yoshi Murata (Weatherhead Fellow, Harvard) in a session on “Leadership, Followership, and Group Culture in a Changing Japan.” As part of the Consulate’s Cultural & Innovative Evenings series, about 20 local residents joined us for a mix of short talks and small-group discussions. Using Barbara Kellerman’s systems theory of leadership, we examined how group experiences—from K–16 education to the workplace—shape dynamics such as senior–subordinate relationships, and how these may be reshaped as Japan welcomes more international workers and residents. I’m proud of my students for sharing their lived experiences and engaging so thoughtfully, and grateful to our guests—including Karina Baum (Boston Public Schools), Mimi Hadi (Embassy of Japan in Iraq), and Miu Takahashi (Nissan North America)—for contributing to the discussion. Here is our slide deck, if interested: https://lnkd.in/g28MjFmJ #Leadership #Japan #GlobalLeadership #CrossCultural #OrganizationalCulture #HigherEducation #USJapan #LeadershipDevelopment #OrganizationalCulture #HigherEd #USJapan #LeadershipDevelopment

My first AERA was a whirlwind and I can't believe it's already coming to a close! It was overwhelming in so many ways, but I feel so blessed and humbled to have learned so much from leading educational scholars and fellow doctoral students on how to better foster supportive spaces for both learners and educators. It's so hard to pick my favorite sessions, but I will definitely take away what I learned on topics like reenvisioning equity in rural spaces, insights on seeing ITAs from an asset-based mindset instead of linguistically deficient, how to better support international student spouses, and just generally how to better support educators and learners that are diverse in so many different ways.

I want to give a huge shout‑out to Yunseo Kim (Yun) and Chaeah Son (Kate), two first‑year undergraduate international students at Northeastern University , who were brave enough to take their community‑based research and turn it into opinion articles for The Huntington News , and both were accepted for publication. This is no small achievement. Writing for a public audience takes courage, clarity, and a willingness to put your ideas into the world - - especially in a second language and as a first‑year student. Yun and Kate did exactly that by asking thoughtful questions, engaging with their communities, and communicating their ideas with purpose and care. Their success is a powerful reminder that willingness to communicate matters. When students are willing to speak up, write boldly, and share their perspectives, meaningful and positive outcomes follow. So proud of this work and of the risks these students took. 👏 Student voices belong in public conversations—and Yun and Kate proved it. #StudentSuccess #InternationalStudents #UndergraduateResearch #WritingInTheDisciplines #CommunityEngagedLearning #TheHuntingtonNews #ProudProfessor #NortheasternUniversity

Just wrapped up a leadership program at Harvard with a group of outstanding high school students from Japan. Deep thanks to Phillips Brooks House Association—the student-led community service hub on campus (where I once worked as a student)—for introducing programs that offer useful models for Japanese students, including the Recent Immigrant Summer Enrichment (RISE) program. As Japan becomes more multicultural in response to demographic decline and new working visas, children of foreign workers are struggling in school because of language barriers. RISE provides ESL and enrichment activities for young immigrant students in Greater Boston, and students from last year’s Japan program have launched a similar initiative in Tokyo, offering Japanese-language and enrichment activities for young foreign residents. Also grateful to the Harvard Undergraduate Japan Initiative. Members gave our students personal campus tours—showing them dorms, favorite study spaces, and other meaningful spots—shared lunch with them, and joined us later in Lehman Hall to help with a Japanese cultural study break for graduate students. The varied interaction helped everyone get to know one another remarkably well in a short period of time, and the Mita students left with new perspectives and greater motivation and confidence to make a difference in the world. Thank you, PBHA and HUJI.
